Spec-Driven Development

Writing the specification before the code, and keeping the two tied together afterwards. Three documents per feature, and an ID system that lets a tool walk from a requirement to the line of code that satisfies it.

Methodology engineering-methodology v0.15.0 Install /plugin marketplace add t-gency/spec-driven-development New here? Start with the quickstart Revised September 2026

1 · Why

The problem it solves, and why the old answer failed.

A team decides to build something. Someone writes a ticket. A developer reads it, fills the gaps with assumptions, and ships. Three weeks later nobody can answer, without opening the code, three basic questions:

  • Was this decided, or did someone assume it?
  • Is the code doing what we agreed, or what was convenient?
  • If we change this, what breaks?

The ticket cannot answer them. It was a task, not a decision record, and it closed. The usual patch is more documentation, and it fails for a specific reason: the documentation is not connected to anything. Nothing breaks when it goes stale, so it goes stale, and then nobody reads it.

Specs are not a new idea. They died once.

And the reason matters: the spec went stale the moment coding started, and nobody could afford to keep it current. Two things changed since.

  • An agent can write most of the document. Cost per spec drops from days to hours.
  • An agent can also audit the code against it. That closes the loop that was always missing.

The second point is the real one. Writing was never the hard part; verifying was. That is what got cheap.

What this is not. Not a template pack, and not a phase gate to satisfy an auditor. A team that adopts the three documents and skips the traceability gets the ceremony without the benefit: three more files to maintain and nothing checking them. Section 3 is the part that pays for the other two.

2 · The three documents

One set per feature. Not per epic, not per release, not per ticket.

DocumentAnswersVoiceLength
Concept NoteWhy, and in what directionDivergent, exploratory2,500–6,000 words
SpecWhat it must do, how it must behaveNormative: every line an obligation4,000–10,000 words
Implementation PlanWhat to build, where, in what orderExecutable8,000–25,000 words, by branch arc

Each document stands on its own, and any stage can be reconstructed from its neighbours. That is a real test: if your Spec cannot be turned into a plan without a meeting, it is underspecified.

The bands count the delivered document, scaffolding included

That matters, because the scaffolding is not small. The Spec template carries ~3,900 words of normative structure before a single placeholder is filled, and §11.5's meta-acceptance-criteria alone contribute ~1,100 words that must survive into the delivered document. A conforming Spec cannot be shorter than its own template.

The earlier band said 1,500–3,500. It predated the traceability layer and was arithmetically impossible to meet. Worth saying out loud, because a limit the templates violate teaches people to ignore limits.

The Plan does not get one number, because its size is set by the branch arc it declares in §7.0 — the nine per-branch subsections and the closing T-N.D1–T-N.D20 block are replicated per branch:

ArcBand
refactor-1, single-branch8,000–12,000 words
two-branch-backend-ui10,000–16,000 words
three-branch-scaffold-core-rollout12,000–19,000 words
five-branch-default, migration-515,000–25,000 words

The upper bounds still carry a rule: if a document runs past its band, split the feature — except for the Plan, where you check the arc first. An oversized Plan is more often a five-branch arc on a two-branch feature than a feature that needs splitting.

The difference a Spec makes

✗ The system must be fast.

✓ The system shall return search results within 300 ms at p95 for datasets under 10,000 records.

Which one can be violated? Only the second. A requirement that cannot be violated is not a requirement.

Each document answers a question the next one is not allowed to reopen. The Concept Note ends by splitting decisions into settled: do not relitigate and decide in the Spec. The Spec does the same toward the Plan. That is the whole mechanism against the most common failure in this work: relitigating a decision three stages downstream, in a code review, with none of the context that produced it.

Two rules hold the set together. Cite, don't paraphrase: when the Spec inherits a decision it writes D-01, not a re-worded version. Empty is legal; silent is not: any section can be empty, but it must say so and why — Security constraints: none — see Concept §5.2. That single rule turns "we forgot" and "we decided not to" into visibly different things.

3 · Traceability

The part that makes it work. Without this, the three documents are ceremony.

Every obligation gets an ID, and the IDs form a chain that runs from a decision to a line of code:

D-01 a decision in the Concept Note
  ↳ TC-002 becomes a constraint in the Spec
    ↳ FR-003 which a requirement must respect
      ↳ S-04 which a scenario exercises
        ↳ a test tagged S-04
          ↳ the code that makes it pass

The bottom two links are what make the rest real.

The scenario ID is embedded in the test itself, in the test name or a native tag — @pytest.mark.scenario("S-04"), it("S-04: recovers the partial turn…"). Not a table in a wiki mapping tests to requirements: a table is a second thing to maintain, and the second thing always rots. A tag in the test file moves with the test, gets deleted with the test, and can be grepped.

Once the IDs are in the documents and in the tests, a tool walks every obligation in the Spec and gives each one exactly one verdict:

VerdictMeaning
IMPLEMENTEDThe code satisfies it, and here is the file and line
PARTIALHalf of it is there; here is which half is missing
ABSENTNothing satisfies it, and here is where it would live
DIVERGENTThe code contradicts it
UNVERIFIABLEIt could not be checked, and here is why

UNVERIFIABLE ranks above ABSENT on purpose: "I could not check" must never be reported as "it is not there." That distinction is what makes the report trustworthy enough to act on.

The audit also runs backwards, looking for public behaviour in the code that no ID sanctions. That is usually the more interesting direction: code nobody specified is either a missing requirement or scope that crept in, and both are worth knowing before someone builds on top of it.

Two rules keep the audit honest

Prose is a claim; code is evidence. Documentation, comments, commit messages, PR descriptions and test names are claims about behaviour. Only the implementation is evidence. A comment that says // validates the token is not proof that a token is validated.

A gate passing is not proof. A failing check is evidence of a gap; a passing check is only evidence that the check passed. A test that asserts nothing, a test whose subject is mocked away, a code path nothing reaches — all of these pass.

Nothing here is technically hard. It did not happen before because the labour was absurd: keeping IDs consistent across three documents and re-verifying the set on every change is weeks of a person's attention per feature, forever. An agent does that pass in minutes, repeatedly, without getting bored on obligation forty-seven.

4 · Adopting it

The methodology says nothing about tickets. Four questions every team has to answer itself.

1 · What is the unit?

our answer: the title carries it

The methodology works one feature at a time; a board works in tickets. You need a name that means the same on both sides. Ours lives in the ticket title: Surface | Feature → Name. The middle segment is the feature, and it names the specs/NNN-feature/ folder. 53 tickets resolved to 18 features. Without something like this, "which tickets belong to this Spec?" has no mechanical answer and the connection is maintained by memory.

How many tickets per feature

One per independently deliverable user story. Not one per feature, and not one per functional requirement.

That is spec-kit's rule and it is the right one: stories are prioritized P1 P2 P3, each independently testable, and P1 alone has to be viable. If you build only that story you still have something worth shipping. That constraint is what prevents a monolithic all-or-nothing spec.

  • Counting FRs is wrong. A requirement is an obligation inside the Spec, not a unit of work. One story spans several FRs, and one FR can serve several stories
  • One ticket per feature is wrong too. It hides the priority order inside the ticket, so nothing can be cut. A feature with three stories has three tickets, and you can drop the third

The ticket and the PR are different axes. The ticket slices by user value, vertically: independently deliverable, prioritized. The PR slices by technical sequencing, horizontally: the Plan's branch arc. One ticket can take several stacked PRs; several tickets never share one.

2 · How does a ticket point at its documents?

two fields in the body

Docs: the feature folder. Satisfies: the Spec IDs the ticket closes. Bugs carry Violates instead: which IDs the current behaviour contradicts, which is the same thing the audit reports as DIVERGENT. If no ID sanctions the behaviour the value is unspecified — and that is a gap in the Spec, not just a bug. This is the entire bridge.

3 · Where do the tasks live?

not on the board

The Plan carries a task checklist meant for an agent. Pushing those onto the board gives you two task systems that drift within a sprint. The ticket is what a person picks up — owner, label, board column; the plan's tasks are the breakdown for whoever executes, and they stay in the document.

4 · What earns the full treatment?

the hardest one

Ask the question of the feature, never of the ticket. That one move is what makes the rest work, and it is a correction: an earlier version derived the answer from what was blocking each ticket, which quietly created a state where a ticket sat on the board waiting for a document nobody had started.

PathWhat runsWhere the issues come from
SpecConcept Note, then Spec. The Plan only if it enters the releaseOut of the approved Spec: one per user story, P1 P2 P3
DirectNothingStraight onto the board: a defect against specified behaviour, or internal work with no user surface
Platform requestNothing from usIt needs a contract from the platform team, not a Spec. It carries a blocked: label and does not count toward the release forecast

There is no fourth case where a ticket waits on a document that does not exist. Asking the question of the feature is what prevents it. What can still block an issue once it exists is a missing mock-up or an unresolved platform dependency — one label each — and an issue carrying any blocked: label does not enter refinement. Result: the full pipeline on 2 or 3 features out of 18.

Where we diverge from spec-kit

spec-kit ships a tasks-to-issues command: the artifacts come first and the issues are generated last, which is the same direction as this. It goes one step further and builds them from the Plan's tasks. We stop at the user story.

The tasks belong to an agent and the story belongs to a person. Putting the tasks on the board gives you two task systems that drift within a sprint.

The honest cost

Between 15,000 and 40,000 words per feature across the three documents, plus real calendar time to write and review them. That is a larger number than this material used to state; the old figure predated the traceability layer and did not survive contact with the templates. Too much for most work, and pretending otherwise is how this gets abandoned: a bug fix does not get a Concept Note, a copy change does not get a Spec.

A team that runs this on everything will quietly stop running it on anything.

It also does not apply when the problem is not understood yet (do discovery first: a Spec written over a guess just makes the guess look official), when the thing is genuinely throwaway, or when nobody will ever run the audit. Without the audit you are buying the cost without the benefit.

A spec nobody verifies decays into fiction. A spec that gets audited is a contract. The only thing that changed is that auditing got cheap.

The gates nobody hands you

What "approved" means. Every template ships as Draft and nothing promotes it. The methodology gives the criteria for not approvable — unresolved questions at requirement level, empty cells in the coverage matrix, blocking review findings — but the act of approving is yours to define. Ours takes four signatures, recorded in the document's own change log: Product, the surface's tech lead, testing, design.

The same feature in two codebases. The methodology assumes one feature, one repo. A product with several clients against one platform breaks that immediately. We keep the documents in each app's repo and have the headers point across at each other, so a change on one side makes the stale side visible. It works, and it runs on human discipline: nothing mechanical enforces it.

Order of adoption. Pick the naming bridge first, before writing any document: it is cheap now and expensive to retrofit across a live board. Then add the two body fields to your ticket templates, even empty. Then run the full pipeline on one feature: the most expensive one you have, not the easiest — an easy feature will not surface the problems. Only then decide the tiering, when the cost is a number instead of a guess. And run the audit before the second feature: if nobody ever runs it, stop there, because the rest is documentation theatre and a good ticket is cheaper.

5 · Plugins and skills

What the difference is, and how to install them.

A skill is a folder of instructions that teaches an agent to do one job well. A plugin is the package that ships a set of skills together, versioned, so a team installs them with one command. Skill is the capability; plugin is the delivery mechanism. You never install a skill on its own.

A skill is a SKILL.md whose front matter names it and describes when it applies. That description is not documentation: it is the routing table. The agent reads every installed skill's description and loads the one that matches what you asked, which is why you invoke a skill in plain language and never type its name — and why a vague description means the wrong skill loads, or none does. When a skill misfires, its description is usually the bug, not its instructions.

StageSkillWhat it does
Authorstaged-engineering-docWrites or derives any of the three documents, through guided Q&A plus codebase research
Presentthree-p-visualizerRenders a feature as a Product / Process / Project explainer
Queryspec-answersAnswers questions about a documented feature, citing IDs
Verifyspec-conformanceAudits the code against the Spec, forward and backward

staged-engineering-doc is the one you will use most, and it does not one-shot a document: it researches the codebase first, asks what it cannot ground, and marks what stays unresolved as [OPEN-Q] rather than guessing.

Security is already covered, and it is not in this plugin

three skills, every control anchored to a standard the reader can download

SkillCovers
secure-devThreat modelling, authentication and authorization (including object- and property-level), sessions, injection and output encoding, CSRF / SSRF / CORS, cryptography, secret handling, error handling, rate limiting, security logging, supply chain, and the AI / agent / MCP overlay
secure-container-imagesDockerfiles and Containerfiles, multi-stage builds, non-root, capabilities, read-only root filesystem, image scanning, SBOM and signing
production-readiness-gateThe go/no-go over a complete feature, with a vulnerability gate. An engineering assessment, not a compliance certification and not an approval authority

What each control is anchored to

AnchorUsed for
OWASP ASVS v5.0The requirement set, and the L1/L2/L3 assurance ladder our P1–R2 types map onto
OWASP Top 10:2025 · API Security Top 10 2023 · CWE Top 25Naming a defect precisely enough to test for it
NIST SP 800-63B · SP 800-218 (SSDF) · SP 800-218AAuthentication assurance; lifecycle practices; the generative-AI profile
CIS Docker Benchmark · NIST SP 800-190Container build and runtime hardening
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025The AI / agent / MCP overlay
CVSS v4.0 · EPSS · CISA KEVThe vulnerability gate

Two things follow from anchoring everything to public sources, and both are improvements. A client can verify our work — every threshold is either cited or explicitly labelled a T-Gency default they are free to replace with their own policy. And the gaps become visible: rotation cadence, log retention, remediation SLAs and exception approval levels are ours, and we say so.

That last point is worth saying out loud in a client room: these are our defaults; if you have a policy, we run against yours.

Where they belong is the whole point, and it is not at the end:

WhenWhichWhy
Writing the Specsecure-dev, starting with the threat modelSo NFR-* and TC-* come from a real control list and a real threat list, not from intuition. Security shapes the WHAT
Phase 2, completenesssecure-dev, secure-container-imagesImplementing the constraints the Spec already committed to. Nothing new is discovered here
Before the PRproduction-readiness-gateThe go/no-go over the complete feature, on evidence

Running only the last one turns security into a veto at the most expensive moment, and the one most likely to get waived under deadline.

Known gaps, stated rather than implied

  • Infrastructure as code and Kubernetes beyond the container security context: no Terraform, NetworkPolicy or cluster RBAC coverage
  • Mobile and desktop clients: none
  • Model safety and evaluation — whether a model produces harmful output — as opposed to the security of the system around the model
  • Privacy engineering beyond data minimisation and retention: no data mapping, subject-rights workflow or transfer analysis

Multi-tenant row-level security used to be on this list. It is now covered in secure-dev §3.2, which requires the tenant predicate to be enforced in the data layer and a test that proves a cross-tenant read fails. A checklist that hides its edges is worse than a short one.

The three live in skills/, deliberately outside the plugin: they are meant to be taken and adapted, not installed as-is. Copy them into your repo's .claude/skills/ and they load automatically.

Installing it

This repository is itself the marketplace. Two lines, typed by a human inside Claude Code — they are client slash-commands, so an agent cannot run them for you:

/plugin marketplace add t-gency/spec-driven-development
/plugin install engineering-methodology@tgency-method

Point the first line at wherever your copy lives. To pick up a later version, /plugin marketplace update tgency-method.

Three things to check before blaming the command. The install is per machine, not per repo — a new laptop needs it again. Private repositories are unreliable here: marketplace add clones over git, and against a private repo it can prompt for credentials, time out, or register the marketplace with no plugins and no visible error — authenticate first if the repo is not public. And a wrong owner or repo reads as "marketplace not found", which looks like the plugin does not exist rather than like a typo.

Which version a document was written under is not a detail — it decides which rules that Spec was approved against. So a document cites a commit, never a branch: a link to main will misrepresent, three weeks from now, what was actually agreed. The plugin is versioned, at 0.15.0 today, and it carries its own decision log (MD-*) and open questions (EVO-*).

This copy is a mirror, and it says so

The plugin is developed in a private engineering repository and mirrored into plugins/engineering-methodology/ so that this repo is installable on its own. UPSTREAM.md records which upstream commit this copy corresponds to, and CI fails when the two disagree.

A deliberate compromise, worth naming rather than hiding: a single source of truth beats a mirror, but a mirror that says which commit it is — and that breaks the build when it drifts — beats a copy nobody can date. If you are adopting this, you have no upstream: delete UPSTREAM.md and let your repo be the source of truth.

6 · The delivery loop

How a feature actually moves from idea to merged code. From the platform team, who run it today.

Two principles decide everything downstream. WHAT before HOW: a feature's value is decided in the Concept Note and the Spec, not in the code. Prototype first, then completeness: get a version that works and show it to Product; only after they confirm the direction do you give the feature completeness.

Phase 1 · PrototypePhase 2 · Completeness
GoalA working prototype Product can react toProduction-grade, complete feature
FocusFunctional behaviour: FR-* and scenariosSecurity, performance, completeness
NFR-* / TC-*Captured in the Spec, scheduledImplemented and verified
TriggerReady when localhost proves the happy pathStarts only after Product sign-off

The non-functional requirements are written into the Spec in Phase 1; they are just not built yet. They are not discovered later and they are not optional. Deferring the work is not the same as deferring the decision, and conflating the two is how "we'll add security later" happens.

Who authors the WHAT

Product owns the WHY and the scope; everyone else shapes it, and each role lands in a different part of the Spec. Four authors from the start beat four signatures at the end.

The ten steps

Each one a plain-language instruction to a coding agent. Steps 1 to 6 are Phase 1; 7 to 10 are Phase 2.

The prompts that drive it

Worth copying nearly verbatim, because the constraints in them are load-bearing.

  • Concept Note — "Draft a concept note for {feature}. Research the codebase first, and ask me whatever you can't ground." The second clause is what stops invention
  • Spec — "Turn this concept note into a spec. Keep the focus on the WHAT, and enumerate the variants for every scenario." Variants are where happy-path-only Specs get caught
  • Implement — "Implement the whole plan end to end. Commit locally as you go, but do NOT push and do NOT open the PR: stop when it's ready to verify on localhost." Nothing is pushed, so the session can run unattended

You do not type skill names. Every step is a plain-language instruction and the right skill loads from its description.

The pre-PR gate, four checks. Coherence against the Spec, audited and reconciled. Enough end-to-end coverage asserting on the real DOM. Sibling Specs, ADRs and docs updated in the same change. A security review over the complete feature, not the prototype. This is where the traceability finally gets enforced.

We adopted the platform team's layout rather than the methodology's default: documents are committed to specs/NNN-feature/ as concept-note.md, spec.md and implementation-plan.md. The methodology explicitly says to mirror whatever convention a repo already has, and a shared shape is what lets one person read across four codebases.

7 · Branching and PRs

Four long-lived branches, each bound to an environment and a publish channel.

BranchEnvironmentChannelRule
mainstagingreleaseTagged. The last step before production
release/*qarcCut from develop. Candidate fixes only
developdevdevDeploys on every merge
feature/*——Pull-request CI and local. Nothing else
hotfix/*——Verified on its PR, then straight to staging

Feature branches cut from develop and squash back into it, so its history reads as a list of features. A release branch is cut when a version is ready and from then on accepts candidate fixes only: that is the entire point of cutting it, and the rule most often bent. Every commit on a release branch is forwarded back to develop, or a fix made during stabilization reappears as a regression in the next version. A hotfix branches from main, not develop, so it never picks up whatever is half-finished.

Channels are not environments. The channel is what CI publishes — dev, rc, release; the environment is where it runs. One branch produces one channel that lands in one environment, and a build is never promoted by being re-tagged into a different channel: it gets rebuilt from the branch that owns that channel.

Stacked PRs

A feature ships as several pull requests stacked on each other, not one large one. How many follows the Implementation Plan's branch arc, sized to the feature: one branch for a refactor, two for backend plus UI, five for a cross-service pair or a data migration.

  • One issue per user story, and every PR in the stack links to it: that issue is the home for the story — progress, blockers, decisions, PR history. A feature with three stories has three issues, each with its own stack
  • The last PR carries Closes #NNN, only the last, or the issue closes early
  • Each PR sits behind a feature flag, so a partially merged stack is never a broken product
  • Merge bottom-up, keeping each branch current with its parent and with main

Every PR carries a conventional title, a link to the issue, and a ## Verified by section naming the tests. Not "tested locally": the test names. Merging bottom-up is the tedious part, and it is a good candidate for a background agent loop.

The Spec-Drive gate. A feat pull request needs its committed Spec, with its FR-*, S-* and AC-*, and CI checks it. Advisory first, required later; a genuine exception is declared with a no-spec: marker rather than by quietly omitting it — the same declared-none-visible rule the methodology applies everywhere. Without this gate the rest is voluntary, and traceability that nothing enforces decays at exactly the speed of deadline pressure.

What we have to decide

This model comes from the platform repo, our client surfaces do not all run it today, and adopting it is not free:

  • Four long-lived branches need four environments. A surface without a QA environment cannot run release/* meaningfully
  • Stacked PRs need review discipline. Five small PRs reviewed slowly is worse than one large PR reviewed fast
  • The Spec-Drive gate needs the Specs to exist first. Turning it on before that is a gate everyone learns to bypass

The sequencing that follows: the gate goes on last, after the documents exist and the branch model is running. Turning it on early teaches the team that gates are obstacles rather than agreements.

8 · The documentation system

The three documents are not the whole story. This is the taxonomy around them.

A feature Spec answers "what should this do". It does not answer "why is the whole system built this way", "what did we learn before we specified it", or "how does an operator restart it at 3am". The platform repo has a full taxonomy for that, and the organising idea is not subject matter: it is how the document changes over time.

PathWhat it isLifecycle
README.mdThe front doorUpdated with the behaviour it describes
specs/NNN-slug/**The per-feature working setLives with the feature branch
docs/specs/**Design intent, for engineers and agentsCarries a status banner; kept as the record
docs/site/**Shipped behaviour, for usersWritten when a feature ships
docs/adrs/**One-time architectural decisionsImmutable once accepted: superseded, never edited
docs/investigation/**Pre-spec research, audits, post-mortemsDated. A snapshot, never retro-edited
docs/conventions/**How we write code hereLiving: fixed in the PR that changes the pattern
docs/runbooks/**Operator playbooksUpdated with the operation they describe

Sorting by lifecycle rather than by topic is what stops the same fact from living in two places and disagreeing. A decision is immutable, a convention is living, research is a dated snapshot: three different rules, three different folders.

Specs are not docs

A spec describes proposed or in-progress design, for engineers and agents. A doc describes shipped, working behaviour, for users. Never let a spec quietly become the user documentation: when a feature ships, its spec gets status: implemented and a durable doc is written. The spec stays as the record of what was intended; the doc says what exists.

Collapsing the two is how a document ends up describing a design that shipped differently and nobody notices, because it reads like documentation.

Every spec opens with one of five states: draft · proposed · accepted · implemented · superseded. That closes a hole in the methodology, where every template says Draft and nothing ever promotes it out. superseded is what lets a document be retired without being deleted.

ADRs are not Concept Note decisions. A D-* is feature-scoped and lives with its feature. An ADR is cross-cutting and one-time: which database, which identity provider, which multi-tenancy model. And it is immutable once accepted: you do not edit an ADR when the decision changes, you write one that supersedes it. A decision log you can rewrite is not a decision log. The platform repo has 26; we have none, which means every cross-cutting decision our client surfaces have made lives in someone's memory or in a thread.

The rule that makes the whole thing hold: a behaviour change is not done until the docs that describe that behaviour change with it, in the same PR. Not a follow-up ticket. The reasoning is the argument against "we'll document it later": documentation that lags the code is worse than none, because it is confidently wrong and readers act on it. And the escape hatch is the familiar one: if no doc applies, say so in the PR description. "No docs needed: internal refactor, no behaviour change" is a complete answer. Silence is not.

Anything countable from the repo is generated, not maintained. Generated blocks sit between markers and are rebuilt from the real source; a CI check fails on a stale block; the generator is fail-closed, so adding a service without a description aborts the build and names what you have to document. That is the good idea — a new component cannot reach main while remaining invisible in the README. The rule generalises: if you find yourself hand-maintaining a list that could be counted from the repo, generate it instead.

Seeds for the other four types

seeds/ has a starting point for each: a seed skill that teaches an agent to write that document type well, a template, and a README for the destination folder, so whoever opens docs/adrs/ learns the rules without reading this.

seeds/adr/  seeds/investigation/  seeds/runbook/  seeds/site-doc/

Starting points, not finished products. Install one, use it for a month, edit it to match what your team actually does. The description in the front matter is the routing table: that is the field to get right when adapting, and the one to suspect when a skill does not fire.

What we should adopt, in order

  • The status vocabulary. Five states, one banner per spec. Cheapest thing here and it closes a real hole
  • docs/investigation/. We already have the content with nowhere to put it: the platform API analysis, the design-audit findings, the migration study
  • The docs-change-in-the-same-PR rule, with our own lookup table. No tooling needed to start: it is a review habit
  • ADRs. Ours would start at three or four: the platform dependency, the shared design system, two chat components in parallel
  • Generated blocks. Last, and only where we already hand-maintain a list that drifts

The first three cost nothing but agreement. The last two cost engineering time, and neither is worth doing before the first three are habits.

Writing rules worth stealing verbatim. English only in the committed file, whatever language the conversation happens in. State what is true now, not what changed — changelogs live in git. Link, do not copy: one fact, one home, because a restatement is a future contradiction. Delete confidently: a section describing something that no longer exists is a bug. Do not invent counts: a number you could have counted from the repo belongs in a generator. And in review, treat missing documentation the same as a missing test.

9 · Our issue standard

One team's answer to section 4, on a real board. Take the shape, not the vocabulary.

GitHub is the single source of truth

The backlog and the issues live in the repo, next to the code, so that task → commit → PR → release traceability is native and agents pick up context automatically. Each repo has its board; the expected access for the whole team is Write.

The boundary with the legacy tracker is clean: the legacy tracker stays tied to maintenance of the previous major version, GitHub holds the new work. No ticket lives in both tools.

Three paths, and the template decides which

PathWhenBefore codingTemplate
SpecNew or user-visible behaviour. Touches permissions, org and project context, contracts, multi-tenancy or telemetryThe pipeline in specs/NNN-feature/Feature
DirectA defect on already-specified behaviour, or internal work with no user surfaceNothing. Security and QA gates still applyBug
Platform requestSomething in the platform that does not exist or is not documentedDescribe the contract neededPlatform request

Title convention and labels

The format is Surface | Feature → Name. Every other dimension is a label, never in the title, so it stays readable. The middle segment is the feature, and it names the specs/NNN-feature/ folder.

DimensionValuesWhat for
surface:web-chat web-design cowork code iOS ipados android crossSeparate squads inside shared repos. The only vocabulary that changes per repo
origin:product clients c-level marketWho is asking. No clear external requester → product
blocked:needs-conceptnote needs-spec design platformWhich artifact is missing
type:feat fix chore spike decisionRecommended, not required

Every blocked: label names a missing artifact, never a team. Which team produces it is a separate question with a separate answer, and one that changes: the label would go stale. Priority is not a label either, it is the org-level Issue field.

Platform tickets are requests, not commitments

  • A pure platform ask carries blocked:platform and says so in its body
  • It does not count in the squad forecast or in the release capacity
  • A feature that depends on an unresolved one does not enter refinement
  • They are opened in the repo of the surface that needs them, not in the platform repo, so the team sees its own dependency on its own board

Templates, not a documented convention

The structure is encoded as GitHub Issue Templates (forms): required fields validate themselves and labels apply automatically per template, so an issue is valid by construction instead of free text someone fixes afterwards. Four of them: Feature, Platform request, Bug, plus config.yml, which disables blank issues and gives the private path for vulnerabilities.

Required fields, derived from what the flow already demands: acceptance criteria in Gherkin; permissions and org/project context; response contracts and multi-tenant behaviour; UX states (empty, loading, error); telemetry where it applies; and the platform dependency classification — known, agreed stub, or unknown.

Entry condition for refinement, in one line: an issue with any blocked: label does not enter. The labels map one-to-one onto the three conditions — approved Spec, validated mock-up, classified platform dependency — so the queue is filtered on the board instead of read issue by issue. Unknown does not enable planning.

The human gates

The delivery loop's pre-PR gate is mechanical. These four are people, and they stay:

  • Product & Design, Security Review, QA Review, and Human Review before merge
  • Automated SAST runs in parallel with them, not instead of them

Known gap: Product & Design and Human Review are exactly where Spec defects surface, not implementation ones. The rejection reason should be typed, and a Spec gap routed back to the Concept Note with a version bump, instead of bouncing to implementation like every other rejection.
